content.title: Can we be good without believing in God?
content.summary: No one is righteous by nature. God's image remains, and common grace is real.

answer.text: Yes, in the everyday sense. People who do not believe in God love their children, keep promises, give generously and risk their lives for strangers, and Scripture expects this: every person bears God's image and has a conscience. Christians should say so plainly. The question hides three senses of “good”: doing what benefits others, which unbelievers often do; knowing a standard of goodness that binds everyone, which raises the question of what grounds it; and being righteous before God, which Scripture says none of us is by nature. In that third sense sin affects the whole person, and outward kindness cannot make us right with God. By common grace, unbelievers can love their children, act generously and do things that benefit their neighbours. These acts do not earn salvation or constitute the God-pleasing righteousness that comes through faith in Christ. We must keep those meanings of “good” distinct.

reasoning.text: The Bible's verdict includes all fallen humanity, not just unbelievers. Christians are saved sinners, not people who were naturally better than their neighbours.

Sin has corrupted God's image in us without erasing it. What Reformed theology calls total depravity means that sin affects every faculty; it does not mean that everyone commits every possible evil or is as wicked as they could be. Baptists of every view confess that we inherit a nature inclined toward sin (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article III), though they differ on how far the fall disables the will.
God restrains evil and gives gifts beyond the church. Real benefit to a neighbour is distinguishable from an act proceeding from faith, according to God's Word and for God's glory.

conclusion.text: An unbeliever can perform outwardly beneficial acts, but no sinner can become righteous before God by those acts. Our need is Christ, whose righteousness is received by faith.

sections.text: Genesis grounds the protection of human life in God's image even after the fall. James condemns cursing people made in God's likeness. We must honour that dignity without treating it as proof of an unfallen heart. Conscience bears witness to accountability; it does not remove our guilt.
sections.title: God's image is dignity, not innocence

sections.text: God's kindness and restraint help explain civic virtue outside the church. They do not regenerate the heart or turn helpful conduct into merit. Even believers' imperfect works are accepted only through Christ. The gospel therefore removes boasting while calling us to grateful obedience.
sections.title: Common grace is not saving grace

sections.text: The moral argument is a further question, not a substitute for the biblical account of sin. God is holy and his law expresses his righteous character. Humanists also affirm ethical responsibility; we should represent that claim accurately while asking what grounds it. Their moral seriousness does not establish a right standing before God.
sections.title: Then ask what makes morality binding

sections.text: When someone asks whether we can be good without God, they usually mean two things. First: do people who reject God keep promises, tell the truth and care for the weak? Plainly they do, and a Christian who denies it is not being faithful to Scripture, which says that Gentiles without the law "do by nature what the law requires" and that their consciences accuse or defend them. Second: if there is no God, is anything really good or evil at all, or only useful or approved? The first is a question about behaviour, and the answer is yes. The second is a question about foundations, and it is where the real disagreement lies.
sections.title: What the sceptic is really asking

sections.text: Andrew Fuller, the English Baptist pastor who helped send William Carey to India, wrote against the deists of his day in 1799. He began by granting the point the sceptic cares about: "The greatest enemies of Christianity would still be thought friendly to morality." No one, he said, defends cruelty or treachery as such; even those who excuse a vice must first give it a better name. Fuller's argument was not that unbelievers are always worse people, but that a God without moral character, the deist's God, cannot explain the moral sense everyone shows, and that "no being is beloved for his greatness, but for his goodness".

citations.locator: Part I, introduction and chapter I, pp. 9–11

sections.title: An old Baptist observation

sections.text: Whether morality needs God is a question of its own, with serious answers on both sides: the theist's case from moral obligation and human value, the secular realist's case that moral facts need no foundation, and the debunker's case that evolution shaped our moral sense. That argument is set out at length in the essay "Does morality need God?", with Plato's old dilemma in a short answer of its own. This page keeps to the question in its title.
sections.title: Where the moral argument is weighed

content.objection: Doesn't this deny the kindness of people who do not believe?

reply.text: No. Feeding someone really benefits them, and neglecting that duty is worse. The question is whether the act meets God's whole standard, including the heart and its ultimate end. Scripture does not permit us to turn relative civic goodness into innocence before a holy God. Nor does it permit Christians to look down on people whose mercy may shame our conduct.

limit.text: The sinlessness of Christ is not an exception we may forget: he alone is our perfectly righteous Saviour. Believers do become truly renewed and do works God accepts in him, but never establish their own saving merit.

prompt.text: When we say someone is good, do we mean that they benefit others, or that they are righteous before God—and how does Christ answer our deeper need?

passages.note: No one is righteous by nature
Even sinners do good to others
Without faith we cannot please God
The law written on the heart

heldBy: many atheists and humanists, answering Christian apologists
objections.objection: When Christians say no one is good without God, they are calling their atheist neighbours wicked. That is insulting, and it is false: many unbelievers live better lives than many believers.

reply.text: If a Christian says that, the complaint is just. Scripture does not say unbelievers are worse than believers; it says all have sinned, believers included, and that sinners still do good to those who do good to them. The claim this page makes is narrower: no one, Christian or not, is righteous before God by their own record, and so everyone, Christian or not, needs Christ. That levels the ground. It gives a believer no room to look down on anyone.

heldBy: evolutionary accounts of ethics, such as Sharon Street's
objections.objection: Our moral sense evolved because cooperation helped our ancestors survive. Kindness and fairness need no God to explain them; natural selection explains them.

reply.text: Evolution may explain how creatures came to feel the pull of fairness. Whether that pull tracks anything true is another question, and several secular philosophers grant that it is a hard one: if our judgements were shaped only for survival, it is not obvious why they would be true. Christians can accept that God made us through means while holding that conscience is a witness, not merely an instinct. The essay on the moral argument weighs this objection in full.

heldBy: Christopher Hitchens, in his 2009 debate with William Lane Craig and in his writings
objections.objection: Religion does not make people good. Religious people have done terrible things in God's name, and believers behave no better than anyone else.

reply.text: Much of the charge is true, and Scripture says so before the critic does: judgement begins with the household of God, and Jesus warned that many who call him Lord he never knew. Christianity does not claim that believers are morally superior. It claims that Christ is righteous and that he forgives and remakes sinners. Where his followers fail, they fail by his standard, not by a standard borrowed from the critic.
